The video displays grainy, black-and-white archival footage of an early biplane on a flat, open field. Initially, the aircraft is shown on the ground near a tall wooden launch structure, with several people standing nearby. As the narration states, "And so we are left with the story of the Wright brothers," the scene transitions to the plane moving along the ground and then lifting into the air. The narrator continues, "When they first flew in front of a movie camera, we have believed their version of history, that the Wright brothers flew first at Kitty Hawk in 1903." The footage follows the biplane as it gains altitude and flies low over the landscape, with a line of trees visible in the background, before the clip ends with the aircraft in flight.
ASR: And so we are left with the story of the Wright brothers. When they first flew in front of a movie camera, we have believed their version of history, that the Wright brothers flew first at Kitty Hawk in 1903.

As the narration explains that these are the first moving pictures of a Wright plane, the men continue their approach across the muddy terrain. The scene then transitions to a modern, dimly lit museum exhibit featuring a large, full-scale replica of a Wright biplane suspended from the ceiling by wooden poles. Below the aircraft, a long white display case contains documents, and the narration notes that by this time, the Wright brothers had secured a lucrative aviation patent for their control system.
ASR: to get a modified version of their biplane into the air. These first moving pictures of a Wright plane were taken in 1908. By now the Wright brothers had taken out a lucrative aviation patent for their control system.

As the tablet remains on screen, a narrator states that for the Wright brothers, the endeavor seemed to be less about inventing the aeroplane and more about making money.
ASR: [Brown] For the Wright brothers, it seems to have not been so much about inventing the aeroplane as about making money.

As these images are shown, the narration explains that "they needed light-weight engines for their gliders, just like the ones invented by Whitehead."

The video displays a close-up view of a newspaper article discussing early aviation experiments. The camera slowly pans across the text, which details the work of inventors Gustave Whitehead and W. D. Custead in Bridgeport, Conn. As the view moves over the paragraph describing Whitehead's "flying machine" with wings that soar like a bird, the narration states, "He has demonstrated that his machine can fly." The text on screen further clarifies that while Whitehead has shown his machine can fly, he does not claim it can be a commercial success, contrasting this with Custead's work on an airship for transportation.
ASR: "He has demonstrated that his machine can fly."

As a man speaks about the price of truth and the role of museums, the camera pans across the aircraft's structure. The scene then cuts to the man standing in a hangar in front of a yellow biplane, continuing his statement. Following this, a narrator questions whether the Wright brothers or Gustave Whitehead truly kick-started the age of aviation. The video transitions to a historical reenactment showing two men in early 20th-century attire standing in a large workshop, followed by a man in a bowler hat working on an aircraft outdoors. The segment concludes with a shot of a biplane flying through a cloudy sky with the sun shining brightly.

The scene then transitions to a wider side profile of the biplane, highlighting its long wingspan and dual propellers, with a figure standing in the distance to the right. Finally, the camera presents a direct head-on view of the aircraft, clearly revealing the horizontally mounted engine and the low-lying pilot position. As these close-ups are shown, the narration explains that the design features a horizontally mounted engine and a low-lying pilot, noting that the aircraft would not resemble three blobs when viewed from a distance.
ASR: Close-ups of the Wright brothers' 1903 flyer show a horizontally mounted engine and a low-lying pilot, nothing that would look like three blobs from a distance.
